notes.front: What is the Azure portal?
notes.back: A web-based, unified console for creating and managing all your Azure resources through a graphical user interface.
notes.explanation: You can build, manage and monitor anything from a simple web app to a complex cloud deployment there.
notes.example: Like online banking, where you point and click through your accounts, but for your whole Azure estate.
notes.source: Azure portal documentation: What is the Azure portal?
notes.evidence: The Azure portal is a web-based, unified console that you can use to create and manage all your Azure resources. By using the Azure portal, you can manage your Azure subscription through a graphical user interface. You can build, manage, and monitor everything from simple web apps to complex cloud deployments in the portal.

notes.front: What is an Azure portal dashboard?
notes.back: A customisable view in the Azure portal focused on the resources in your subscription that matter most to you.
notes.explanation: The portal gives you a default dashboard, which you can customise to bring frequently used resources into a single view.
notes.example: Like the home screen of a phone, arranged with the apps you use most, but showing Azure resources.
notes.source: Azure portal documentation: What is the Azure portal?, “Dashboard”
notes.evidence: Dashboards provide a focused view of the resources in your subscription that matter most to you. The portal provides a default dashboard to get you started. You can customize this dashboard to bring resources you frequently use into a single view, or to display other information.

notes.front: What is Azure Cloud Shell?
notes.back: An interactive, authenticated terminal in the browser for managing Azure resources, using Bash or PowerShell.
notes.explanation: It runs on a temporary host provided per session and per user, so there is nothing to install locally.
notes.example: Like a hotel business centre's computer that is already signed in to your work systems, but reached through any browser.
notes.source: Azure Cloud Shell documentation: What is Azure Cloud Shell?
notes.evidence: Azure Cloud Shell is an interactive, authenticated, browser-accessible terminal for managing Azure resources. It provides the flexibility of choosing the shell experience that best suits the way you work, either Bash or PowerShell. Cloud Shell runs on a temporary host provided on a per-session, per-user basis.

notes.front: What is the Azure CLI (Azure Command-Line Interface)?
notes.back: A cross-platform command-line tool for connecting to Azure and running administrative commands on Azure resources.
notes.explanation: You can type its commands interactively in a terminal or put them into a script.
notes.example: Like texting precise instructions to a builder instead of pointing at things on site.
notes.source: Azure CLI documentation: What is the Azure CLI?
notes.evidence: The Azure Command-Line Interface (CLI) is a cross-platform command-line tool to connect to Azure and execute administrative commands on Azure resources. It allows the execution of commands through a terminal using interactive command-line prompts or a script.

notes.front: What is Azure PowerShell?
notes.back: The collection of official Microsoft PowerShell modules for managing Azure resources.
notes.explanation: It needs PowerShell, a command-line shell and scripting language, and runs commands interactively or as scripts.
notes.example: Like an add-on pack of Azure commands for a shell you may already use to manage Windows.
notes.source: Azure PowerShell documentation: What is Azure PowerShell?
notes.evidence: Azure PowerShell is the product name for the collection of official Microsoft PowerShell modules for managing Azure resources. It requires PowerShell, a command-line shell and scripting language. You can use Azure PowerShell interactively by running commands from PowerShell or creating and executing scripts that consist of multiple commands.

notes.front: What is a cmdlet?
notes.back: A command-let: one of the commands you run in Azure PowerShell to carry out a management task in Azure.
notes.explanation: You can run a cmdlet on its own for a one-off change, or combine several to handle a larger job.
notes.example: Like a single recipe step, such as “whisk the eggs”, that can be used alone or strung into a full recipe.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe tools for interacting with Azure, “What is Azure PowerShell?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Copilot in Azure?
notes.back: An artificial-intelligence assistant that gives Azure administrators guidance in natural language, in the context of their work.
notes.explanation: Teams use it to speed up tasks such as exploring services, understanding configuration options and drafting commands or scripts.
notes.example: Like an experienced colleague at your elbow who answers questions in plain English, but whose advice you still check.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe tools for interacting with Azure, “AI-assisted operations with Copilot in Azure”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Azure Resource Manager (ARM)?
notes.back: The deployment and management service for Azure: the management layer through which you create, update and delete resources.
notes.explanation: After deployment you also use its features, such as access control, locks and tags, to secure and organise resources.
notes.example: Like a building's front desk, which checks everyone's pass and routes every request to the right department.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What is Azure Resource Manager?
notes.evidence: Azure Resource Manager is the deployment and management service for Azure. It provides a management layer that helps you to create, update, and delete resources in your Azure account. You use management features like access control, locks, and tags to secure and organize your resources after deployment.

notes.front: What is Azure Arc?
notes.back: A platform that gives consistent Azure management and governance to resources on premises and in other clouds.
notes.explanation: Without it, each environment and cloud tends to have its own management tools, which makes control across them hard.
notes.example: Like a single smart-home app that controls devices from several brands, not just its own.
notes.source: Azure Arc documentation: Azure Arc overview
notes.evidence: Each environment and cloud possesses its own set of management tools, and new DevOps and ITOps operational models can be hard to implement across resources. Azure Arc simplifies governance and management by delivering a consistent multicloud and on-premises management platform.

notes.front: What is infrastructure as code (IaC)?
notes.back: Defining the infrastructure to deploy in code, which is kept in a source repository and versioned like application code.
notes.explanation: Because the infrastructure code is part of the project, anyone on the team can run it to deploy similar environments.
notes.example: Like a recipe card that lets any cook reproduce the dish, instead of a chef cooking from memory.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What are ARM templates?
notes.evidence: In code, you define the infrastructure that needs to be deployed. The infrastructure code is part of your project. Just like application code, store the infrastructure code in a source repository and version it. Anyone on your team can run the code and deploy similar environments.

notes.front: What is an ARM template?
notes.back: A JavaScript Object Notation file that declares the infrastructure and configuration to deploy for a project.
notes.explanation: ARM templates are how you put infrastructure as code into practice for Azure solutions.
notes.example: Like an architect's drawing that shows the finished house, leaving the builders to work out the order of work.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What are ARM templates?
notes.evidence: To implement infrastructure as code for your Azure solutions, use Azure Resource Manager templates (ARM templates). The template is a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) file that defines the infrastructure and configuration for your project.

notes.front: What is Bicep?
notes.back: A domain-specific language that uses declarative syntax to deploy Azure resources.
notes.explanation: You define the infrastructure in a Bicep file and reuse that file through the development lifecycle to deploy it repeatedly and consistently.
notes.example: Like shorthand for a long legal form: same meaning, far fewer words.
notes.source: Bicep documentation: What is Bicep?
notes.evidence: Bicep is a domain-specific language that uses declarative syntax to deploy Azure resources. In a Bicep file, you define the infrastructure you want to deploy to Azure and then use that file throughout the development lifecycle to repeatedly deploy that infrastructure. Your resources are deployed in a consistent manner.

notes.front: What are two everyday tasks you can do in the Azure portal?
notes.back: Any two, among others: set up a new database; increase a virtual machine's compute power; monitor monthly costs.
notes.explanation: The portal also lets you review all available resources and create new ones with guided wizards.
notes.source: Azure portal documentation: What is the Azure portal?
notes.evidence: For example, you can set up a new database, increase the compute power of your virtual machines, and monitor your monthly costs. You can review all available resources and use guided wizards to create new ones.

notes.front: Why does the failure of one Azure datacentre not take the Azure portal down?
notes.back: The portal has a presence in every Azure datacentre.
notes.explanation: Being present everywhere also helps avoid network slowdowns by keeping the portal close to users.
notes.source: Azure portal documentation: What is the Azure portal?
notes.evidence: It has a presence in every Azure datacenter. This configuration makes the Azure portal resilient to individual datacenter failures and helps avoid network slowdowns by being close to users.

notes.front: The Azure portal updates continuously and needs {{c1::no downtime}} for maintenance.
notes.explanation: It is designed for resiliency and continuous availability.
notes.source: Azure portal documentation: What is the Azure portal?
notes.evidence: The Azure portal is designed for resiliency and continuous availability.

notes.front: Can you share a customised Azure portal dashboard with colleagues?
notes.back: Yes. You can publish customised dashboards and share them with other users in your organisation.
notes.explanation: You can also create further dashboards purely for your own use.
notes.source: Azure portal documentation: What is the Azure portal?, “Dashboard”
notes.evidence: You can create other dashboards for your own use, or publish customized dashboards and share them with other users in your organization.

notes.front: Through which two Azure command-line tools does Cloud Shell give you instant, already-authenticated access to your resources?
notes.back: The Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell.
notes.explanation: Cloud Shell signs you in securely and automatically, and comes with popular command-line tools already installed.
notes.source: Azure Cloud Shell documentation: What is Azure Cloud Shell?, “Authenticated and configured Azure workstation”
notes.evidence: Cloud Shell comes with popular command-line tools and language support. Cloud Shell automatically securely authenticates for instant access to your resources through the Azure CLI or Azure PowerShell cmdlets.

notes.front: Who manages the machine behind Azure Cloud Shell?
notes.back: Microsoft does, so you have nothing to install or maintain.
notes.explanation: It is offered as an authenticated and configured Azure workstation.
notes.source: Azure Cloud Shell documentation: What is Azure Cloud Shell?, “Authenticated and configured Azure workstation”
notes.evidence: Microsoft manages Cloud Shell so you don't have to.

notes.front: An Azure Cloud Shell session times out after {{c1::20 minutes}} without interactive activity.
notes.explanation: Its host is temporary and provided per session, per user.
notes.source: Azure Cloud Shell documentation: What is Azure Cloud Shell?
notes.evidence: Cloud Shell runs on a temporary host provided on a per-session, per-user basis. Your Cloud Shell session times out after 20 minutes without interactive activity.

notes.front: Where does Azure Cloud Shell keep your files between sessions?
notes.back: In your `$HOME` location, on a 5-gigabyte file share.
notes.explanation: The host is temporary and per session, while the file share keeps your files.
notes.source: Azure Cloud Shell documentation: What is Azure Cloud Shell?
notes.evidence: Cloud Shell runs on a temporary host provided on a per-session, per-user basis. Your Cloud Shell session times out after 20 minutes without interactive activity. Cloud Shell persists your files in your `$HOME` location using a 5-GB file share.

notes.front: What does it cost to use Azure Cloud Shell?
notes.back: The machine hosting it is free; the storage account holding its file share incurs regular storage costs.
notes.explanation: Cloud Shell needs a storage account to host the mounted Azure Files share.
notes.source: Azure Cloud Shell documentation: What is Azure Cloud Shell?, “Pricing”
notes.evidence: Use of the machine hosting Cloud Shell is free. Cloud Shell requires a storage account to host the mounted Azure Files share. Regular storage costs apply.

notes.front: Where can you run the Azure CLI?
notes.back: Installed locally on Linux, macOS or Windows; in a browser through Azure Cloud Shell; or inside a Docker container.
notes.explanation: Wherever it runs, you can use it interactively or from scripts.
notes.source: Azure CLI documentation: What is the Azure CLI?
notes.evidence: locally on Linux, macOS, or Windows computers. It can also be used from a browser through the [Azure Cloud Shell][12] or run from inside a Docker container.

notes.front: How do you automate a repetitive task with the Azure CLI?
notes.back: Put the commands into a shell script, using your chosen shell's script syntax, and run the script.
notes.explanation: For one-off work you instead type commands at the shell prompt, for example in Bash or cmd.exe.
notes.source: Azure CLI documentation: What is the Azure CLI?
notes.evidence: For interactive use, you first launch a shell such as cmd.exe on Windows, or Bash on Linux or macOS, and then issue a command at the shell prompt. To automate repetitive tasks, you assemble the CLI commands into a shell script using the script syntax of your chosen shell, and then you execute the script.

notes.front: Which PowerShell module is the current, recommended version of Azure PowerShell, and on which platforms does it run?
notes.back: The Az module; it is cross-platform, running on Windows, Linux and macOS.
notes.explanation: It includes thousands of commands that control almost every aspect of Azure.
notes.source: Azure PowerShell documentation: What is Azure PowerShell?, “The Az PowerShell module”
notes.evidence: The current version of Azure PowerShell is the **Az** PowerShell module. It's the recommended PowerShell module for managing Azure resources with PowerShell on all platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. It includes thousands of commands that control almost every aspect of Azure.

notes.front: You find an online example that uses the AzureRM PowerShell module. Should you follow it?
notes.back: No. AzureRM is the previous generation of Azure PowerShell: deprecated, unsupported and not recommended.
notes.explanation: Its commands use the `*-AzureRM*` format, which makes such examples easy to spot.
notes.source: Azure PowerShell documentation: What is Azure PowerShell?, “The AzureRM PowerShell module”
notes.evidence: While you might find examples online that use the **AzureRM** PowerShell module, it's the previous generation of Azure PowerShell. It's deprecated, no longer maintained or supported, and not recommended.

notes.front: What do you gain by capturing a set of cmdlets in a script?
notes.back: The process becomes repeatable and can be automated.
notes.explanation: Combined cmdlets can handle work as large as setting up and tearing down connected resources, or deploying a whole infrastructure.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe tools for interacting with Azure, “What is Azure PowerShell?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do the Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell differ in what they can do?
notes.back: They are functionally equivalent; the main difference is the syntax of their commands.
notes.explanation: Since their capabilities and access are so similar, the choice mostly comes down to which command language you know best.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe tools for interacting with Azure, “What is the Azure CLI?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Should you apply what Copilot in Azure suggests straight to production?
notes.back: No. Validate its recommendations, confirm permissions and review deployment changes first.
notes.explanation: At a fundamentals level, Copilot is best treated as an operational assistant rather than the decision-maker.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe tools for interacting with Azure, “AI-assisted operations with Copilot in Azure”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does Azure Resource Manager do with a request sent from any Azure tool?
notes.back: It authenticates and authorises the request, then forwards it to the appropriate Azure service.
notes.explanation: Because every request goes through the same interface, you see consistent results and capabilities in all the tools.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What is Azure Resource Manager?, “Consistent management layer”
notes.evidence: When you send a request through any of the Azure APIs, tools, or SDKs, Resource Manager receives the request. It authenticates and authorizes the request before forwarding it to the appropriate Azure service. Because all requests are handled through the same API, you see consistent results and capabilities in all the different tools.

notes.front: Is there anything you can do in the Azure portal that PowerShell or the Azure CLI can't?
notes.back: No. All capabilities in the Azure portal are also available through PowerShell and the Azure CLI, among other routes.
notes.explanation: New functionality in the underlying interfaces reaches the portal within 180 days of its first release.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What is Azure Resource Manager?, “Consistent management layer”
notes.evidence: All capabilities that are available in the Azure portal are also available through PowerShell, the Azure CLI, REST APIs, and client SDKs. When APIs introduce new functionality, this reflects in the portal within 180 days of initial release.

notes.front: Which Resource Manager benefit lets you deploy, manage and monitor all the resources of a solution together instead of one at a time?
notes.back: Managing the solution's resources as a group.
notes.explanation: Resource Manager treats the solution's resources as a unit rather than handling each individually.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What is Azure Resource Manager?, “The benefits of using Resource Manager”
notes.evidence: Deploy, manage, and monitor all the resources for your solution as a group, rather than handling these resources individually.

notes.front: What can you define in Resource Manager so that resources are deployed in the correct order?
notes.back: The dependencies between resources.
notes.explanation: Resource Manager uses those dependencies to decide what must exist before what.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What is Azure Resource Manager?, “The benefits of using Resource Manager”
notes.evidence: Define the dependencies between resources so they're deployed in the correct order.

notes.front: Why can you apply access control to all Azure services through Resource Manager?
notes.back: Azure role-based access control is natively integrated into the management platform.
notes.explanation: Every request passes through Resource Manager, where access control is built in.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What is Azure Resource Manager?, “The benefits of using Resource Manager”
notes.evidence: Apply access control to all services because Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC) is natively integrated into the management platform.

notes.front: How does Resource Manager help clarify an organisation's billing?
notes.back: You can view costs for a group of resources that share the same tag.
notes.explanation: Tags applied through Resource Manager also organise all the resources in a subscription logically.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What is Azure Resource Manager?, “The benefits of using Resource Manager”
notes.evidence: Apply tags to resources to logically organize all the resources in your subscription. * Clarify your organization's billing by viewing costs for a group of resources that share the same tag.

notes.front: If Resource Manager fails in one Azure region, does that stop it working in other regions?
notes.back: No. Resource Manager has a separate instance in each Azure region.
notes.explanation: It is also spread across availability zones where a region has them, and isn't taken down for maintenance.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What is Azure Resource Manager?, “Resiliency of Resource Manager”
notes.evidence: Resource Manager has a separate instance in each Azure region, meaning that if a Resource Manager instance fails in one region, this doesn't affect the service's availability in another region

notes.front: How does Azure Arc let you manage non-Azure resources together with your Azure ones?
notes.back: It projects existing non-Azure and on-premises resources into Azure Resource Manager.
notes.explanation: You can then manage virtual machines, Kubernetes clusters and databases as if they were running in Azure.
notes.source: Azure Arc documentation: Azure Arc overview
notes.evidence: Manage your entire environment together by projecting your existing non-Azure and/or on-premises resources into Azure Resource Manager. * Manage virtual machines, Kubernetes clusters, and databases as if they are running in Azure.

notes.front: Which resource type lets Azure Arc manage Windows and Linux physical machines and virtual machines hosted outside Azure?
notes.back: Servers (and virtual machines).
notes.explanation: Arc can also provision, resize and delete such virtual machines.
notes.source: Azure Arc documentation: Azure Arc overview
notes.evidence: Servers and virtual machines: Manage Windows and Linux physical servers and virtual machines hosted outside of Azure. Provision, resize, delete, and manage virtual machines

notes.front: Which resource type lets Azure Arc attach and configure container orchestration clusters running anywhere, across several supported distributions?
notes.back: Kubernetes clusters.
notes.explanation: Several Kubernetes distributions are supported, wherever the clusters run.
notes.source: Azure Arc documentation: Azure Arc overview
notes.evidence: Kubernetes clusters: Attach and configure Kubernetes clusters running anywhere, with multiple supported distributions.

notes.front: Which Azure Arc resource type lets you run a managed database instance on premises, at the edge or in other public clouds, using Kubernetes?
notes.back: Azure data services.
notes.explanation: They run on the infrastructure of your choice, through Kubernetes.
notes.source: Azure Arc documentation: Azure Arc overview
notes.evidence: Azure data services: Run SQL Managed Instance on-premises, at the edge, and in public clouds using Kubernetes and the infrastructure of your choice.

notes.front: Why do agile teams turn to infrastructure as code?
notes.back: They deploy repeatedly and need their infrastructure in a reliable state, managed through one process with application code.
notes.explanation: As infrastructure joined the iterative process, the division between operations and development disappeared.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What are ARM templates?
notes.evidence: They need to repeatedly deploy their solutions to the cloud, and know their infrastructure is in a reliable state. As infrastructure became part of the iterative process, the division between operations and development disappeared. Teams need to manage infrastructure and application code through a unified process.

notes.front: How does a declarative template differ from imperative deployment commands?
notes.back: A declarative template states what you intend to deploy; imperative commands spell out the sequence of steps to create it.
notes.explanation: In the template you specify only the resources to deploy and their properties.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What are ARM templates?
notes.evidence: The template uses declarative syntax, which lets you state what you intend to deploy without having to write the sequence of programming commands to create it. In the template, you specify the resources to deploy and the properties for those resources.

notes.front: What do you specify in an ARM template?
notes.back: The resources to deploy and their properties, and optionally the resource group to deploy them into.
notes.explanation: Because the syntax is declarative, you describe the result rather than the programming steps to reach it.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What are ARM templates?
notes.evidence: The template uses declarative syntax, which lets you state what you intend to deploy without having to write the sequence of programming commands to create it. In the template, you specify the resources to deploy and the properties for those resources. You can also specify in which resource group those resources are deployed.

notes.front: Which ARM template benefit means deploying the same template many times gives the same resource types in the same state?
notes.back: Repeatable results: templates are idempotent.
notes.explanation: One template can represent the desired state, instead of separate templates for each update.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What are ARM templates?, “Why choose ARM templates?”
notes.evidence: Templates are idempotent, which means you can deploy the same template many times and get the same resource types in the same state. You can develop one template that represents the desired state, rather than developing lots of separate templates to represent updates.

notes.front: Which ARM template benefit means Resource Manager creates interdependent resources in the correct order, in parallel where it can?
notes.back: Orchestration.
notes.explanation: Parallel creation makes deployments finish faster than one-by-one deployment.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What are ARM templates?, “Why choose ARM templates?”
notes.evidence: Resource Manager orchestrates the deployment of interdependent resources so they're created in the correct order. When possible, Resource Manager deploys resources in parallel, so your deployments finish faster than serial deployments.

notes.front: Which ARM template benefit lets you break a template into smaller reusable pieces, or nest one template inside another?
notes.back: Modular files.
notes.explanation: The smaller components are linked together at deployment time.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What are ARM templates?, “Why choose ARM templates?”
notes.evidence: You can break your templates into smaller, reusable components and link them together at deployment time. You can also nest one template inside another template.

notes.front: Which ARM template benefit lets you add PowerShell or Bash deployment scripts to a template?
notes.back: Extensibility.
notes.explanation: Deployment scripts let you complete your end-to-end environment setup in a single template.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What are ARM templates?, “Why choose ARM templates?”
notes.evidence: With deployment scripts, you can add PowerShell or Bash scripts to your templates. The deployment scripts extend your ability to set up resources during deployment.

notes.front: When does Resource Manager start deploying an ARM template?
notes.back: Only after the template passes validation.
notes.explanation: Checking first makes the deployment less likely to stop in a half-finished state.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What are ARM templates?, “Why choose ARM templates?”
notes.evidence: Your template is deployed only after passing validation. Resource Manager checks the template before starting the deployment to make sure it succeeds. Your deployment is less likely to stop in a half-finished state.

notes.front: What happens to a Bicep file when you deploy it?
notes.back: It is automatically converted to an ARM template.
notes.explanation: Bicep offers the same capabilities as ARM templates, but with syntax that's easier to use.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What are ARM templates?
notes.evidence: We introduced a new language named Bicep that offers the same capabilities as ARM templates but with a syntax that's easier to use. Each Bicep file is automatically converted to an ARM template during deployment.

notes.front: Which language does Microsoft recommend you look at if you are considering infrastructure as code options for Azure?
notes.back: Bicep.
notes.explanation: The recommendation appears in the ARM templates overview itself.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What are ARM templates?
notes.evidence: If you're considering infrastructure as code options, we recommend looking at Bicep.

notes.front: How does a Bicep file compare with the equivalent JavaScript Object Notation ARM template?
notes.back: The Bicep file is more concise and easier to read, and needs no prior knowledge of programming languages.
notes.explanation: Both are declarative, specifying which resources and properties to deploy.
notes.source: Bicep documentation: What is Bicep?, “Benefits of Bicep”
notes.evidence: When compared to the equivalent JSON template, Bicep files are more concise and easier to read. Bicep doesn't require prior knowledge of programming languages. Bicep syntax is declarative and specifies which resources and resource properties you want to deploy.

notes.front: Do you pay for Bicep or any premium Bicep features?
notes.back: No. Bicep is free and open source, and Microsoft Support supports it.
notes.explanation: Being free means there are no premium capabilities to buy.
notes.source: Bicep documentation: What is Bicep?, “Benefits of Bicep”
notes.evidence: **No cost and open source**: Since Bicep is free, you don't pay for premium capabilities. Microsoft Support supports it.

notes.front: A practice manager at a dental surgery has never used a command line. She needs to check this month's Azure costs and give a virtual machine more compute power, by pointing and clicking. Which tool suits her?
notes.choices:
A) The Azure CLI
B) An ARM template
C) The Azure portal
notes.back: C: the Azure portal.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the Azure CLI is a command-line tool. B is wrong: a template is code describing resources to deploy.
notes.explanation: The portal is a graphical interface in which you can monitor costs and increase virtual machines' compute power.
notes.source: Azure portal documentation: What is the Azure portal?
notes.evidence: By using the Azure portal, you can manage your Azure subscription through a graphical user interface. You can build, manage, and monitor everything from simple web apps to complex cloud deployments in the portal. For example, you can set up a new database, increase the compute power of your virtual machines, and monitor your monthly costs.

notes.front: An administrator on a borrowed laptop, where she can't install software, needs to run a few Azure CLI commands straight away. What should she use?
notes.choices:
A) An Azure portal dashboard
B) Install Azure PowerShell locally
C) Azure Cloud Shell in the browser
notes.back: C: Azure Cloud Shell in the browser.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: she can't install software. A is wrong: a dashboard is a view of resources, not a command line.
notes.explanation: Microsoft manages Cloud Shell, and it is already authenticated for the Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell.
notes.source: Azure Cloud Shell documentation: What is Azure Cloud Shell?, “Authenticated and configured Azure workstation”
notes.evidence: Microsoft manages Cloud Shell so you don't have to. Cloud Shell comes with popular command-line tools and language support. Cloud Shell automatically securely authenticates for instant access to your resources through the Azure CLI or Azure PowerShell cmdlets.

notes.front: A script contains the line New-AzResourceGroup -Name Payroll -Location uksouth. Which tool is it written for?
notes.choices:
A) Azure PowerShell
B) The Azure CLI
C) Bicep
notes.back: A: Azure PowerShell.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the Azure CLI's equivalent starts with az group create. C is wrong: Bicep files declare resources rather than calling commands.
notes.explanation: The Azure CLI form of the same command begins az group create, while New-AzResourceGroup is the PowerShell form.
notes.source: Azure CLI documentation: What is the Azure CLI?, “PowerShell syntax comparison”
notes.evidence: az group create --name \<ResourceGroupName> --location eastus |New-AzResourceGroup -Name \<ResourceGroupName> -Location eastus

notes.front: A Linux engineer who writes Bash every day must automate Azure tasks, and asks whether the Azure CLI can do everything Azure PowerShell can. What is the best advice?
notes.choices:
A) Use neither; only the portal can automate
B) Learn PowerShell; the Azure CLI lacks many features
C) Use the Azure CLI; the tools are functionally equivalent
notes.back: C: use the Azure CLI; the tools are functionally equivalent.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the tools differ mainly in syntax, not capability. A is wrong: both command-line tools can be scripted.
notes.explanation: With such similar capabilities, the choice mostly comes down to the language you already know.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training: Describe tools for interacting with Azure, “What is the Azure CLI?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: One admin resizes a database in the Azure portal; another makes the same change with Azure PowerShell. Why do both get the same result and the same permission checks?
notes.choices:
A) Each tool keeps its own copy of the rules
B) The portal secretly runs PowerShell
C) Both requests go through Azure Resource Manager
notes.back: C: both requests go through Azure Resource Manager.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the tools are separate routes into the same management layer. A is wrong: authentication and authorisation happen once, in Resource Manager.
notes.explanation: Resource Manager authenticates and authorises every request, and all requests are handled through the same interface.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What is Azure Resource Manager?, “Consistent management layer”
notes.evidence: It authenticates and authorizes the request before forwarding it to the appropriate Azure service. Because all requests are handled through the same API, you see consistent results and capabilities in all the different tools.

notes.front: A supermarket chain runs Kubernetes clusters in the back office of each store and wants to configure and govern them from Azure, as if they ran there. Which service fits?
notes.choices:
A) Azure Arc
B) Azure Cloud Shell
C) Bicep
notes.back: A: Azure Arc.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: Cloud Shell is a browser terminal, not a way to bring outside resources under Azure management. C is wrong: Bicep is a deployment language.
notes.explanation: Azure Arc projects non-Azure resources into Resource Manager so they can be managed as if running in Azure.
notes.source: Azure Arc documentation: Azure Arc overview
notes.evidence: Manage your entire environment together by projecting your existing non-Azure and/or on-premises resources into Azure Resource Manager. * Manage virtual machines, Kubernetes clusters, and databases as if they are running in Azure.

notes.front: A firm wants Azure Arc to manage a physical Linux machine in a rented data hall. Under which Azure Arc resource type does it fall?
notes.choices:
A) Azure data services
B) Kubernetes clusters
C) Servers
notes.back: C: servers.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: that type covers Kubernetes clusters, not a single machine. A is wrong: that type runs managed database instances.
notes.explanation: The servers type covers Windows and Linux physical servers and virtual machines hosted outside Azure.
notes.source: Azure Arc documentation: Azure Arc overview
notes.evidence: Servers and virtual machines: Manage Windows and Linux physical servers and virtual machines hosted outside of Azure.

notes.front: A software house rebuilds identical test environments several times a week, and any developer should be able to do it. What practice fits?
notes.choices:
A) Careful manual clicking in the portal each time
B) Infrastructure as code kept in the source repository
C) A written checklist on the team wiki
notes.back: B: infrastructure as code kept in the source repository.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: manual steps don't give reliable repeatable builds. C is wrong: a checklist is still followed by hand.
notes.explanation: With the infrastructure defined in versioned code, anyone on the team can run it to deploy similar environments.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What are ARM templates?
notes.evidence: Just like application code, store the infrastructure code in a source repository and version it. Anyone on your team can run the code and deploy similar environments.

notes.front: File X lists a virtual network and two virtual machines with their settings and no steps. File Y is a PowerShell script that runs 30 cmdlets one after another to build them. Which is declarative?
notes.choices:
A) Both
B) File Y
C) File X
notes.back: C: file X.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: a sequence of commands is imperative. A is wrong: only X states the end result without the steps.
notes.explanation: Declarative syntax states what you intend to deploy without writing the sequence of commands to create it.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What are ARM templates?
notes.evidence: The template uses declarative syntax, which lets you state what you intend to deploy without having to write the sequence of programming commands to create it.

notes.front: A colleague hands you a declarative JavaScript Object Notation file that names storage accounts to deploy, with their properties and target resource group. What is it?
notes.choices:
A) A Bicep file
B) An ARM template
C) An Azure CLI script
notes.back: B: an ARM template.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: Bicep uses its own language, not JavaScript Object Notation. C is wrong: a CLI script is a sequence of commands.
notes.explanation: An ARM template is a JavaScript Object Notation file that defines the infrastructure and configuration for a project.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What are ARM templates?
notes.evidence: The template is a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) file that defines the infrastructure and configuration for your project.

notes.front: A team finds its JavaScript Object Notation templates verbose and wants a more concise declarative language with the same capabilities, still deploying through Resource Manager. What should it adopt?
notes.choices:
A) Bicep
B) Azure PowerShell scripts
C) Azure portal dashboards
notes.back: A: Bicep.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: scripts are imperative, not declarative. C is wrong: dashboards display resources and don't deploy them.
notes.explanation: Bicep has the same capabilities as ARM templates with easier syntax, and each Bicep file becomes an ARM template on deployment.
notes.source: Azure Resource Manager documentation: What are ARM templates?
notes.evidence: We introduced a new language named Bicep that offers the same capabilities as ARM templates but with a syntax that's easier to use. Each Bicep file is automatically converted to an ARM template during deployment.
